steps.title: Filling the cylinder
steps.prompt: A cylinder can burn only the oxygen that reaches it. As altitude increases and the air pressure falls, predict what happens to the mass of air a naturally aspirated cylinder of fixed volume can draw in. Then follow the air in through the induction system, and the burned gas out through the exhaust.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 133-142 and the glossary on PDF p. 476, supported by EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 205-216. The prediction is qualitative; no power-loss rate is given.

mediaPlan.rationale: A prediction prompt that sets up the whole lesson: charge mass depends on pressure.

steps.title: Air mass sets the power
steps.prompt:
Fuel can burn only in the oxygen the cylinder gets. So the weight of the air that reaches the cylinder sets how much fuel can burn, and how much power the engine makes.

Every intake stroke draws in the same volume, but a volume of thin air holds less oxygen than the same volume of dense air. What counts is the weight of the charge. Thin air at altitude, hot air, humid air, a restriction in the intake or warm carburettor heat air lower it, and so lower the power. A supercharger or turbocharger raises it.

Volumetric efficiency compares the volume of charge the engine draws in, corrected for temperature and pressure, with its piston displacement. Lesson 13 shows how altitude, temperature and humidity change the charge.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 56 (volumetric efficiency is a comparison of the volume of air-fuel charge, corrected for temperature and pressure, inducted into the cylinders to the total piston displacement of the engine; a naturally aspirated engine's pistons displace the same volume each time) and PDF p. 131 (carburettor heat makes the air expand and decrease in density, which reduces the weight of the charge delivered to the cylinder and causes a noticeable loss of power because of decreased volumetric efficiency). That the oxygen sets how much fuel can burn is the lesson's explanation.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: From scoop to cylinder
steps.prompt: Air is collected by a scoop in the cowling, passes an air filter, and reaches the fuel metering device, a carburettor or a fuel injector. The throttle plate controls how much air flows, and the pressure after it is the manifold pressure, measured in inches of mercury, which sets the power. An intake manifold with long curved pipes then carries the air, or the air-fuel mixture, to each cylinder. A balance tube evens out the pressure between the two sides so that every cylinder gets its share. On a fuel-injected engine the fuel is injected at the intake port just before the intake valve.
steps.alt: FAA exploded drawing of a downdraft balanced induction system: a throttle body, hoses, an induction manifold assembly, four intake manifold tubes and their intake gaskets, all labelled.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 129-130 (scoop, filter, fuel metering device, throttle and manifold pressure, balance tube; updraft and downdraft systems; fuel injected at the intake port), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 71-72 and 195-196. A general example, not a drawing of the GTSIO-520-H, whose induction system comes later in the lesson.

mediaPlan.rationale: The labelled drawing shows the parts of a balanced intake manifold that the text names.

steps.title: Sharing the air
steps.prompt:
The induction manifold shares the air, or the air-fuel mixture, between the cylinders. On an engine with a carburettor the manifold carries the mixture. On a fuel-injected engine like the GTSIO-520-H it carries air only, and the fuel is injected at the inlet port of each cylinder.

The shares must be equal. If they are not, some cylinders run lean and others rich. A carburettor setting must be rich enough to burn in the leanest cylinder, so poor distribution makes the whole engine run richer than it needs to.

A leak at the cylinder end of an intake pipe leans out that cylinder, which may overheat, fire intermittently or cut out.

The long curved pipes and the balance tube in the figure of the last step are there to give every cylinder its fair share.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 401 (the induction manifold provides the means of distributing air, or the air-fuel mixture, to the cylinders; on a fuel-injection engine the manifold handles only air and the fuel is delivered to a nozzle in each cylinder; a carburettor setting must be rich enough to supply a combustible mixture for the leanest cylinder, so if fuel distribution is poor the overall mixture must be richer; a leak at the cylinder end of an intake pipe leans out the mixture, and the affected cylinder may overheat, fire intermittently or cut out) and PDF p. 129 (the balance tube).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: The intake stroke
steps.prompt: At 90° of the cycle the piston is moving down and the intake valve is open, so the charge flows in. The thin coloured trace through the intake port is the model's gas cue: it shows the direction of flow, not a measured flow. Notice how little time there is: the intake valve is open for only part of the cycle, and the whole charge must pass the valve in that time.
steps.note: Documented four-stroke sequence from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48. The mechanism pose is profile-checked; the valve and gas cues are an ideal teaching profile, not GTSIO-520-H timing or CFD. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The shared 720-degree cylinder profile puts the learner at the intake stroke with the valve open.

steps.title: Dirt, ice and heat
steps.prompt: The induction system has three enemies. Dust is hard and abrasive, and an engine that breathes it wears its cylinder walls, rings and bearings, so the air passes a filter that must be cleaned or replaced on schedule. Ice can form in clouds, fog, rain or humid air, in three kinds: impact ice, fuel evaporation ice and throttle ice, and it can cut off the charge or change the air-fuel ratio. Carburettor heat takes warm air from around the exhaust to melt it, but warm air is less dense, so it reduces the weight of the charge and the power. Use it only as needed.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 131-132 (three types of induction icing; carburettor heat takes warm air from around the exhaust and reduces the weight of the charge and the power; dust damage and filter servicing), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 195-196. The handbook says on PDF p. 130 that carburettor heat leans the mixture and on PDF p. 131 that the mixture becomes richer, so this step does not state a direction.

mediaPlan.rationale: A maintenance-relevance step; the hazards are explained in words before the boosted systems.

steps.title: Driven supercharger
steps.prompt: Trace the mechanically driven supercharger from the crankshaft drive to the compressor impeller and the intake manifold. The compressor raises the density of the charge, but the engine itself has to supply the power to turn it. Compressing air also heats it, so some installations need to cool the charge before it reaches the cylinders.
steps.alt: FAA drawing of an internally driven supercharger induction system, with the intake air duct, carburettor heat valve, carburettor, supercharger, intake pipe and manifold pressure gauge labelled.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 133-135 (internally driven superchargers, mechanical drive, the charge gains heat as it is compressed). Figure 3-10 is the primary visual source.

mediaPlan.rationale: A real induction diagram makes the engine-driven compressor visible.

steps.title: Turbo energy path
steps.prompt: Open and close the waste gate, then trace the exhaust energy through the turbine and the compressor. Notice how the compressor discharge pressure, the pressure before the throttle (upper-deck pressure) and the manifold pressure are related, without treating them as identical at every operating condition.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 135-142 (a turbine driven by exhaust gas turns the compressor; the waste gate controls how much exhaust reaches the turbine). The animation explains control relationships qualitatively and does not calculate boost for a real engine.

mediaPlan.rationale: Opening and closing the waste gate makes the control relationship causal, not just labelled.

steps.title: Where the turbocharger sits
steps.prompt: This normalizing installation shows the whole layout in a nacelle. The exhaust from the cylinders is collected and carried to the turbocharger. The compressor air goes into the induction system and on to the intake manifold. Find the alternate air intake: if the air filter clogs, an alternate air door lets the compressor draw air from inside the cowling instead.
steps.alt: FAA cutaway of an engine nacelle with the air intake, alternate air intake, induction system, intake manifold, turbocharger, exhaust system, control system and the throttle and mixture control labelled.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 137 (the turbocharger air induction system consists of a filtered ram-air intake; an alternate air door within the nacelle admits alternate air if the filter clogs) and PDF p. 138 (Figure 3-16). A general example of a small-aircraft installation, not the GTSIO-520-H.

mediaPlan.rationale: A single cutaway shows where the induction and exhaust systems meet at the turbocharger.

steps.title: Normalize or boost
steps.prompt: A normalizing turbocharger makes up for the pressure lost with altitude, up to its critical altitude. It is not used to raise the manifold pressure above 30 inches of mercury. A ground-boosted (sea-level boosted) system can raise it above ambient, to around 40 inches, so the engine can develop more power at sea level than it could without the turbocharger. Critical altitude is the highest altitude, in a standard atmosphere, at which the system can still hold a chosen power or manifold pressure at a given engine speed. The handbook is careful to call only a ground-boosted system a true supercharger. Which kind an engine has depends on its installation and limits.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 133 (normalizing systems are not ground-boost systems and never boost above 30 inches; a true supercharger boosts manifold pressure above ambient), PDF p. 137 (normalizer turbocharger; ground-boosted systems raise manifold pressure above 30 inches to around 40 inches) and PDF p. 140 (the definition of critical altitude).

mediaPlan.rationale: A vocabulary step that keeps normalizing, ground boosting and critical altitude distinct.

steps.title: The GTSIO-520-H induction path
steps.prompt: The GTSIO-520-H is geared, turbocharged, fuel injected and has an intake air intercooler. Follow the numbered parts in the manual's figure: the turbocharger (3) feeds the air throttle (6), a duct (7) carries the air to the intercooler (14), and the intake manifold (17) shares it between the intake tubes (23), one to each cylinder. Compression heats the air a great deal: the handbook gives an example of up to 500 °F leaving a compressor on a 100 °F day, when the allowable air temperature at the throttle inlet is only about 230 to 300 °F. A cooler stops the charge getting close to detonation.
steps.alt: Continental manual figure C-3-2, an exploded drawing of the GTSIO-520-H induction system with the turbocharger, air throttle, air induction duct, intercooler, intake manifold and intake tubes numbered.
steps.credit: Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, Figure C-3-2
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 152 (C-3-2: the engine is geared, turbocharged, fuel injected, with an intake air intercooler) and PDF p. 161 (Figure C-3-2, the -H induction system and its parts list), with the disassembly order on PDF p. 157. The flow order is read from the figure. The handbook (FAA-H-8083-32B, PDF p. 142) describes an aftercooler between the compressor and the air throttle inlet and gives the temperature figures; installations differ, so follow the manual for the engine in front of you.

mediaPlan.rationale: The manufacturer figure for the course engine names every part of its induction path.

steps.title: Altitude compare
steps.prompt: Move the altitude slider and switch between the naturally aspirated, normalizing and ground-boosted modes. Compare the ambient pressure with the manifold pressure each system can hold, and find the altitude beyond which a system can no longer reach its target.
steps.note: Documented relationships from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 133-142, and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 205-216. The graph uses explicitly schematic values and is not performance data for any engine.

mediaPlan.rationale: Moving the altitude makes critical altitude something the learner finds, not just reads.

steps.title: Control and limits
steps.prompt: A turbocharger is controlled by its waste gate, which lets exhaust gas bypass the turbine. On many engines engine oil pressure moves the waste gate: more oil pressure closes it, more gas goes through the turbine and the boost rises. Two controllers share the work, one for full throttle and one for part throttle. Two terms are easy to confuse. Overboost is manifold pressure above the engine's limit, and it can cause serious damage. Bootstrapping is a slow drift of manifold pressure in the controls, which is not harmful to engine life. Limits and procedures come from the data for the installed engine.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 138-142 (waste gate position set by oil pressure in the actuator; density controller and differential pressure controller; overboost versus bootstrapping and overshoot; a pressure relief valve in some systems). This step explains purpose and vocabulary; it gives no operating limits or procedures.

mediaPlan.rationale: A vocabulary and control step; the numbers belong to the installed engine's data.

steps.title: The exhaust stroke
steps.prompt: At 630° the piston is moving up and the exhaust valve is open, pushing the burned gas out. The thin coloured trace through the exhaust port is the gas cue, again only a direction. The exhaust system's first job is to take this hot, poisonous gas away safely, and it also has to survive the heat, corrosion and vibration while doing it.
steps.note: Documented four-stroke sequence from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48 and exhaust-system duty from PDF p. 149 (a scavenging system that collects and disposes of high-temperature, noxious gases safely). The valve and gas cues are an ideal teaching profile, not GTSIO-520-H timing or CFD. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The shared 720-degree profile puts the learner at the exhaust stroke with the exhaust valve open.

steps.title: What the exhaust system does
steps.prompt:
The reciprocating engine exhaust system is fundamentally a scavenging system: it collects the hot, noxious gases the engine discharges and disposes of them. Its first duty is to protect the airframe and the people on board from them.

The exhaust manifold, or the stacks on a simple system, takes the gas from the exhaust port of each cylinder and gathers it. From there it goes on to a tailpipe or ejector, or on a turbocharged engine to the turbine.

The system can do useful work as well. It can drive a turbocharger, heat the cabin and the carburettor air, and draw cooling air through the engine compartment with its ejectors.

It has to resist high temperature, corrosion and vibration while it does all this.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 149 (the reciprocating engine exhaust system is fundamentally a scavenging system that collects and disposes of the high-temperature, noxious gases being discharged by the engine; its main function is to dispose of the gases with complete safety to the airframe and the occupants; it can perform many useful functions, but its first duty is to provide protection against the destructive action of the exhaust gases; modern systems resist high temperatures, corrosion and vibration; on turbosupercharged engines the exhaust gases are collected to drive the turbine; ejectors induce a flow of cooling air through the engine compartment) and PDF p. 150.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Short stack or collector
steps.prompt: There are two kinds of exhaust system. A short stack (open) system lets each cylinder blow out through its own short pipe; it suits non-supercharged and low-power engines where noise does not matter. A collector system gathers the gas from the cylinders into collector tubes. It is used on most large non-supercharged engines and on all turbosupercharged engines, because on those the gas must be collected to drive the turbine. A collector raises the back pressure, the pressure the exhaust has to push against, but on a turbocharged engine the power gained is more than the power lost. The tapered ends of the collectors work as ejectors, drawing cooling air through the engine compartment.
steps.alt: FAA cutaway of a horizontally opposed engine in its nacelle, with red exhaust down-stacks joining collector tubes on each side that run aft to the exhaust ejectors at the firewall.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 149-150 (short stack and collector systems; collector systems on all turbosupercharged engines; back pressure and the turbosupercharging gain; exhaust ejectors and augmenter tube action), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF p. 72.

mediaPlan.rationale: The cutaway shows the stacks, collectors and ejectors in place in a nacelle.

steps.title: Exhaust on an opposed engine
steps.prompt:
On a horizontally opposed engine the exhaust runs along each side. A down-stack leaves each cylinder. The stacks join an exhaust collector tube on each side of the engine, held by ring clamps, and each collector tube ends in an exhaust ejector at the firewall, pointing aft and down. The tapered ends of the collector tubes deliver the gas at the speed that pulls cooling air through the engine compartment.

A cabin heater shroud is fitted around each collector tube.

On a turbosupercharged engine all the gas is collected and sent on to the turbine instead.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 149 and Figures 3-38 and 3-39 (the exhaust system components of a horizontally opposed engine: a down-stack from each cylinder, an exhaust collector tube on each side of the engine, and an exhaust ejector assembly protruding aft and down from each side of the firewall; the down-stacks are connected to the cylinders with high-temperature locknuts and to the collector tube by ring clamps; a cabin heater exhaust shroud is installed around each collector tube; the collector tubes are tapered to deliver the exhaust gases at the proper velocity to induce airflow; on turbosupercharged engines the gases are collected to drive the turbine).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Radial collector ring
steps.prompt: A radial engine has its own pattern. Its collector ring is a welded, corrosion-resistant steel assembly made in sections, each section collecting the exhaust from two cylinders; on the 14-cylinder engine in the figure there are seven. The sections grow in size from the inboard side to the outboard side, where the tailpipe joins the ring. A telescoping expansion joint at the tailpipe lets a section of the ring be removed without taking the tailpipe off.
steps.alt: FAA drawing of the exhaust collector ring of a radial engine: a ring of welded sections joined to short stacks at each cylinder port, graduated in size towards the tailpipe connection.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 150 (radial engine exhaust collector ring: seven sections on a 14-cylinder engine, each collecting from two cylinders, graduated in size; telescoping expansion joint), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF p. 73.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook drawing shows the graduated sections of a collector ring.

steps.title: Mufflers and heat exchangers
steps.prompt: On many single-engine aircraft a shroud around part of the exhaust acts as a heat exchanger. It heats air for the cabin, for windscreen defrosting and for carburettor heat. That makes it a risk: about half of all muffler and heat-exchanger failures are cracks in the heat-exchanger surface, which let exhaust gas into the cabin heat system, a carbon monoxide hazard, or into the induction system, causing overheating and power loss. Inside a muffler, erosion and carbonisation can break baffles loose and block the flow. Blocked or restricted exhaust raises the back pressure and takes power away; backfiring and burning of unburned fuel in the exhaust make these failures more likely.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 149 (shroud heat for the inlet air, cabin heater and windshield defrosting), PDF pp. 151-152 (about half of muffler and heat-exchanger failures are cracks in the heat-exchanger surfaces; carbon monoxide; exhaust drawn into the induction system; internal baffle and diffuser failures restrict the flow and cause partial or complete power loss; backfiring and unburned fuel in the exhaust are contributing factors). Backfiring itself is covered in the Operation Malfunctions lesson.

mediaPlan.rationale: The hazards are chains of cause and effect that read best as text.

steps.title: Back pressure
steps.prompt:
Back pressure is the pressure the exhaust gas has to push against as it leaves the cylinder. With an open exhaust it is about the pressure of the air outside. Anything that restricts the flow raises it.

A higher back pressure leaves more burned gas in the cylinder and makes the engine work harder to push it out, so it costs power.

A collector system raises the back pressure compared with short stacks. A turbocharged engine accepts that, because the gain from turbocharging is greater than the loss. A bayonet stack is shaped to reduce both the back pressure and the noise.

A blocked or restricted exhaust, such as a muffler with broken baffles, raises the back pressure in a way nobody wants, and takes power away.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 149 (the collector system raises the back pressure of the exhaust system; on a turbosupercharged engine the gain in horsepower from turbosupercharging more than offsets the loss from increased back pressure), PDF p. 401 (barometric pressure is the exhaust back pressure on an engine with an open exhaust, 29 inches of mercury in the handbook's example) and the glossary, PDF p. 461 (bayonet stacks decrease both exhaust back pressure and noise). That a higher back pressure leaves more burned gas in the cylinder and costs power is the lesson's explanation, consistent with the handbook's account of partial or complete loss of power from a restricted exhaust (PDF p. 150).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Inspecting the exhaust
steps.prompt: Any exhaust failure is a severe hazard: carbon monoxide in the cabin, loss of power, or fire. Inspect the clamped joints and port connections for leaks, which show as a flat grey or sooty black streak. Look at every weld, bend, clamp, support and gasket for cracks, dents and missing parts. A part that cannot be inspected where it is can be plugged, pressurised to about 2 psi and dipped in water, and any leak shows as bubbles. Never use galvanised or zinc-plated tools on an exhaust system and never mark its parts with a lead pencil: the lead or zinc enters the hot metal, softens it, and causes cracks.
steps.alt: FAA drawing of three types of exhaust system, labelled A, B and C, with red arrows marking the primary areas to inspect at joints, flanges, mufflers and heat-exchanger shrouds.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 150-151 (any exhaust failure is a severe hazard; no galvanised tools or lead pencil marks; leaks show as a flat gray or sooty black streak; inspection of welds, clamps, supports and gaskets; the 2 psi water test; Figure 3-42). This is a recognition lesson: the system manufacturer's data gives the limits and torques.

mediaPlan.rationale: The figure marks where each type of exhaust system is inspected.

steps.title: Turbocharged exhaust
steps.prompt: When there is a turbocharger the exhaust works under much higher pressure and temperature. At altitude the exhaust pressure is held near its sea-level value, so a small leak escapes with torch-like force and can damage nearby structure. Carbon (coke) deposits in the waste gate make it work erratically, and a waste gate that sticks closed causes overboost. Deposits in the turbocharger itself cause a slow loss of power. Periodic de-coking keeps the system efficient, and the cleaning and adjustment follow the manufacturer's instructions.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 152 (exhaust systems with a turbocharger: greatly increased pressure and temperature, torch-like leaks, coke deposits in the waste gate, waste gate sticking closed causing overboost, de-coking, manufacturer's instructions).

mediaPlan.rationale: A short maintenance step that connects the exhaust to the turbocharger control ideas.

steps.title: Exhaust and induction together
steps.prompt:
Induction and exhaust are one breathing path, and each acts on the other. During valve overlap both valves are open, and the pressures on the two sides of the cylinder decide which way the gas goes.

When the manifold pressure is above the back pressure, for example 35 inches of mercury against 29, the difference of 6 inches (3 psi) pushes fresh charge across the cylinder towards the open exhaust and drives the burned gas ahead of it. The cylinder is completely scavenged and fills with fresh charge: overlap gives more power.

When the manifold pressure is below the back pressure, as at idle with 20 inches against 29, the difference runs the other way. Burned gas, or on an open stack fresh air, is drawn back into the cylinder.

The turbocharger links them too: the exhaust drives the compressor that raises the induction pressure.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 401 to 402 and Figure 10-49 (all aircraft reciprocating engines of current design use valve overlap; at a manifold pressure of 35 inches of mercury and a back pressure of 29 inches there is a differential of 6 inches (3 psi), which forces the air-fuel mixture across the combustion chamber toward the open exhaust and forces the remaining exhaust gases ahead of it, giving complete scavenging and increased power; at 20 inches there is a differential of 9 inches (4.5 psi) in the opposite direction, drawing air or exhaust gases into the cylinder through the exhaust port; with collector rings the inflow is inert burned gas, with open stacks it is fresh air that leans out the mixture). The turbocharger link: PDF p. 149 and the earlier steps.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Breathing sets the power
steps.prompt: Trace the whole path in your own words: the scoop, filter and throttle, the intake manifold, the open intake valve, then the exhaust valve, collector and tailpipe, and where a turbocharger takes energy from the exhaust to raise the pressure of the induction air. lessons.title: Performance Calculations
lessons.objective: Calculate an engine's displacement, compression ratio, indicated, brake, friction and thrust horsepower and mean effective pressure from its data, and explain the thermal, mechanical, volumetric and propulsive efficiencies and where the fuel's heat goes.

steps.title: Work and horsepower
steps.prompt: Work is a force acting through a distance: lift one pound one foot and you have done one foot-pound. Power is work done in a given time. James Watt found that a good horse could work at 550 ft-lb every second, which is 33,000 ft-lb every minute, and that became the horsepower. Drag a 100 lb weight 660 ft in 2 minutes with a steady pull of 90 lb and you do 59,400 ft-lb of work, which is 29,700 ft-lb a minute, so you are using 29,700 ÷ 33,000 = 0.9 hp. To find an engine's horsepower, divide the work it does each minute by 33,000.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 48-49 (work = force x distance; the foot-pound; Watt's 550 ft-lb per second or 33,000 ft-lb per minute; the worked example of a 100 lb weight dragged 660 ft in 2 minutes, 0.9 hp), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF p. 37. In watts, one horsepower is 746 W (EASA p. 37).

mediaPlan.rationale: The unit and its definition are the start of every calculation that follows.

steps.title: Size and compression
steps.prompt: The size of an engine is its piston displacement: the area of the piston multiplied by the stroke, for one cylinder, and then by the number of cylinders. The area of the piston is 0.7854 × bore². The 14-cylinder handbook engine, 5.5 in bore and 5.5 in stroke, displaces 130.67 cu in a cylinder and 1,829 cu in in all. The compression ratio is the total volume divided by the clearance volume. A cylinder with a 5.0 in bore, a 3.75 in stroke and a clearance volume of 10.5 cu in sweeps 73.6 cu in, so its ratio is (73.6 + 10.5) ÷ 10.5 = 8.01:1.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 49-50 (piston displacement, the area of a circle, the 14-cylinder example with total displacement 1,829.4 cubic inches; compression ratio) and the course deck (slides 212 and 218: the 5.0 in bore, 3.75 in stroke and 10.5 cu in clearance volume example, 8.01:1). The Power Generation lesson works the same formulas for the GTSIO-520-H.

mediaPlan.rationale: Two formulas the learner already met, restated with new numbers.

steps.title: Indicated horsepower: PLANK
steps.prompt: Indicated horsepower is the power developed in the cylinders, before any friction is taken off. It is found from the pressure in the cylinder. Because the pressure changes through the cycle, an average, the indicated mean effective pressure, is used. The formula spells PLANK: P is that pressure in psi, L the stroke in feet, A the area of the piston in square inches, N the power strokes per minute of one cylinder, and K the number of cylinders. Then ihp = PLANK ÷ 33,000. In a four-stroke engine each cylinder fires once in two turns of the crankshaft, so N is the rpm divided by 2.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 50-52 (indicated horsepower from the indicated mean effective pressure; the mnemonic PLANK; N is the number of power strokes per minute, half the rpm in a four-stroke engine; the cylinder pressure rises on the compression stroke and peaks after top centre, Figure 1-39). The handbook's worked example prints the pressure as 1.65 lb/in2, but its result of 1,069.123 hp needs 165 lb/in2; the lesson uses the corrected number. The example also writes "number of cycles = 12" where it means twelve cylinders.

mediaPlan.rationale: The formula is stated once and then used in the calculator and the worked example.

steps.title: PLANK calculator
steps.prompt: Try the three example engines, then change one thing at a time. Double the stroke, then double the speed, then double the number of cylinders. What happens to the indicated horsepower each time? Which change cannot be made without making the engine bigger? Then move the mechanical efficiency to see how much of the power reaches the propeller.
steps.note: Built for this lesson from the handbook's PLANK formula (FAA-H-8083-32B, PDF pp. 50-52) and the friction horsepower and mechanical efficiency of PDF pp. 53 and 56. The GTSIO-520-H preset uses the manual's bore, stroke, cylinder count and 375 hp at 2275 propeller rpm with a 0.667:1 drive (PDF pp. 152-153); the mean effective pressure is not in the manual and is chosen to match, at an assumed 90 percent mechanical efficiency. It is a teaching calculator, not engine data.

mediaPlan.rationale: Changing one input at a time makes each factor in PLANK something the learner can feel.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.prompt: A four-cylinder, four-stroke engine runs at 2,400 rpm. The bore is 5.0 in, the stroke 4.5 in and the indicated mean effective pressure 135 psi. A = 0.7854 × 5.0² = 19.635 sq in. L = 4.5 ÷ 12 = 0.375 ft. N = 2,400 ÷ 2 = 1,200 power strokes a minute. K = 4. Then ihp = 135 × 0.375 × 19.635 × 1,200 × 4 ÷ 33,000 = 144.6 hp. Write each term down before you multiply: most mistakes are a stroke left in inches or an rpm that has not been halved.
steps.note: Calculation from the course deck (slide 219: four cylinders, four-stroke, 2,400 rpm, bore 5.0 in, stroke 4.5 in, mean effective pressure 135 psi), using the formula of FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 50-52. The deck gives the problem without an answer; the answer is calculated here and checked in the unit tests.

mediaPlan.rationale: A worked calculation the learner can repeat step by step.

steps.title: Brake horsepower and torque
steps.prompt: Brake horsepower is the power the engine delivers to the propeller shaft. It is measured as torque, the force times its distance from the axis, and the speed. A Prony brake clamps a collar on a drum on the shaft, and an arm of known length rests on a scale. If the scale reads 200 lb and the arm is 3.18 ft long, the torque is 200 × 3.18 = 636 lb-ft. The work done per turn is 2π times the torque, so at 3,000 rpm bhp = 2π × 200 × 3.18 × 3,000 ÷ 33,000 = 363 hp. The same bhp can come from more torque at less speed or less torque at more speed.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 52-53 (brake horsepower is the power delivered to the propeller; torque = force x distance; the Prony brake; 200 lb x 3.18 ft = 636 lb-ft; work per revolution = 2 pi x torque; power = work per revolution x rpm, divided by 33,000; horsepower is a function of both torque and rpm). The final figure is calculated from the handbook's example numbers at 3,000 rpm (the handbook's own substitution uses 3,000 rpm).

mediaPlan.rationale: The measurement method and one worked number; the formula follows from the definition of torque.

steps.title: Friction and mechanical efficiency
steps.prompt: The difference between indicated and brake horsepower is the friction horsepower: the power used overcoming the friction of the moving parts, drawing in fuel, pushing out exhaust and driving the oil and fuel pumps and other accessories. On modern engines it may be as much as 10 to 15 percent of the indicated horsepower. The mechanical efficiency is the brake horsepower divided by the indicated horsepower, and for the average aircraft engine it approaches 90 percent. Friction stays about the same at all speeds, so mechanical efficiency is best at the speed that gives maximum bhp. An engine with 200 ihp and 30 fhp delivers 170 bhp, and its mechanical efficiency is 170 ÷ 200 = 85 percent.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 53 (friction horsepower is ihp minus bhp; as high as 10 to 15 percent of the indicated horsepower) and PDF p. 56 (mechanical efficiency = bhp / ihp; friction between moving parts remains practically constant over the speed range, so mechanical efficiency is highest at the rpm of maximum bhp; the average aircraft reciprocating engine approaches 90 percent). The 200 ihp and 30 fhp example is from the course daily quiz (day 5).

mediaPlan.rationale: Definitions and a short example that connect the three kinds of horsepower.

steps.title: Mean effective pressures
steps.prompt: The part of the indicated mean effective pressure that produces brake horsepower is the brake mean effective pressure, BMEP, and the part used against friction is FMEP. They are not real pressures you could measure in a cylinder, but they are useful: they let engines be rated, and limits be set, in terms of the pressure in the cylinder. If the bhp is known, BMEP = bhp × 33,000 ÷ (L × A × N × K). For the GTSIO-520-H, 375 hp at about 3,411 crankshaft rpm, with L = 0.333 ft, A = 21.65 sq in, N = 1,705 and K = 6, gives a BMEP of about 168 psi.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 54 (IMEP, FMEP and BMEP; BMEP = bhp x 33,000 / (L A N K); the worked example of 1,000 bhp on twelve cylinders giving 154.32 lb/in2; they are useful, but not real, physical pressures; one of the basic limits on engine operation is the pressure in the cylinder). The GTSIO-520-H figure is calculated from the manual's bore, stroke, 375 horsepower at 2275 propeller rpm and 0.667:1 drive ratio (PDF pp. 152-153); the manual does not give a BMEP.

mediaPlan.rationale: A definition, the formula and one calculated value for the course engine.

steps.title: Thrust horsepower
steps.prompt: Brake horsepower stops at the propeller shaft. What the aircraft feels is the thrust the propeller makes. Thrust horsepower is the engine and propeller working together. If the propeller were 100 percent efficient, thrust horsepower and brake horsepower would be equal, but the propeller's efficiency changes with engine speed, attitude, altitude, temperature and airspeed, so it never is. An engine that develops 1,000 bhp with an 85 percent efficient propeller gives 850 thrust horsepower. Of the kinds of horsepower, it is the thrust horsepower that decides the performance of the engine and propeller together.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 54 (thrust horsepower is the engine and propeller together; propeller efficiency varies with engine speed, attitude, altitude, temperature and airspeed; the 1,000 bhp and 85 percent example giving 850 thrust hp).

mediaPlan.rationale: One idea, one example.

steps.title: Watts and kilowatts
steps.prompt:
Horsepower is not the only unit of power. The SI unit is the watt: one joule of work every second. Engine power is often quoted in kilowatts, and 1 kW is 1,000 W.

The horsepower of 550 ft-lb every second is 745.7 W. The electrical horsepower is exactly 746 W, and the two are close enough for most work.

kilowatts = horsepower × 0.7457
horsepower = kilowatts × 1.341

The GTSIO-520-H's 375 hp is 375 × 0.7457 = 279.6 kW. A 100 kW motor is 100 ÷ 0.7457 = 134 hp.

Check which horsepower a data sheet means before you convert. Some data give a metric horsepower, which is a little smaller than the one in this course.
steps.note: Documented from OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, section 7.4 Power (the watt as one joule per second and 1 hp = 746 W) and NIST SP 811 Appendix B.8 (1 hp of 550 ft-lbf/s = 745.6999 W; electric horsepower = 746 W exactly). The 550 ft-lb per second horsepower: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 49. The GTSIO-520-H's 375 hp: overhaul manual, PDF p. 152. The remark on a metric horsepower is a caution only; its value is not used in this course.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Converting units
steps.prompt:
Engine data mixes units, and a calculation goes wrong if they are not converted first. Keep a few factors to hand.

Length: 1 in = 25.4 mm. The 5.25 in bore is 133.35 mm.
Mass: 1 lb = 0.4536 kg. The 550.39 lb dry weight is 249.7 kg.
Volume: 1 cu in = 16.387 cm³. 520 cu in is 8,521 cm³, or 8.52 litres.
Pressure: 1 psi = 6.895 kPa. 1 inch of mercury = 3.386 kPa = 0.491 psi.
Power: 1 hp = 0.7457 kW.

Inside a formula, make the units match its terms. In PLANK the stroke must be in feet, so divide inches by 12, and the speed must be power strokes a minute, so halve the rpm. Gas-law temperatures must be absolute, in kelvin or degrees Rankine.
steps.note: Conversion factors from NIST SP 811 Appendix B.8 (1 in = 25.4 mm exactly; 1 lb = 0.4535924 kg; 1 cu in = 16.387064 cm3 from 1.638706 x 10^-5 m3; 1 psi = 6.894757 kPa; 1 inch of mercury = 3.38638 kPa at 32 degrees F; 1 hp = 745.6999 W). The inch of mercury in psi is the quotient (3.386 / 6.895 = 0.491), which agrees with the handbook's 6 inches of mercury being about 3 psi (FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 401). The PLANK units (stroke in feet, N = rpm / 2): PDF p. 51. The -H's bore, displacement and dry weight: overhaul manual, PDF pp. 152 to 153. Absolute temperatures: the Factors Affecting Power lesson.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Where the heat goes
steps.prompt: Burning fuel releases heat, and only part of it becomes power. In this figure about 25 to 30 percent is converted into useful power, 40 to 45 percent leaves with the exhaust, 15 to 20 percent is removed by the cooling fins, and 5 to 10 percent is removed by the oil. The biggest loss is out of the exhaust pipe. Anything that puts more of the heat into work on the piston, or reduces friction, pumping loss, unburned fuel or heat lost to the engine parts, raises the thermal efficiency.
steps.alt: FAA figure of five engines in a row showing where the heat of combustion goes: heat released by combustion, 25 to 30 percent converted into useful power, 40 to 45 percent carried out with the exhaust, 15 to 20 percent removed by the fins and 5 to 10 percent removed by the oil.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 55-56 (Figure 1-42 and its text: 25 to 30 percent to useful power, 15 to 20 percent lost in cooling, 5 to 10 percent lost in overcoming friction, 40 to 45 percent lost through the exhaust). The figure labels the 5 to 10 percent as removed by the oil and the text as friction.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook figure shows the whole heat balance in one picture.

steps.title: Thermal efficiency
steps.prompt: Thermal efficiency is the share of the energy in the fuel that becomes useful work. A pound of fuel gives up about 20,000 BTU, and each BTU is worth 778 ft-lb of work. The brake thermal efficiency uses the brake horsepower: bhp × 33,000 ÷ (fuel burned per minute × heat value × 778). An engine that delivers 85 bhp for an hour on 50 lb of fuel of 18,800 BTU per pound has a brake thermal efficiency of 0.23, or 23 percent. The handbook says reciprocating engines are only about 34 percent thermally efficient. That figure and the 25 to 30 percent that reaches useful power fit together if friction takes the difference. A higher compression ratio raises the efficiency, but it also raises the cylinder head temperature and the risk of detonation.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 55-56 (thermal efficiency; 20,000 BTU per pound and 778 ft-lb per BTU; the brake thermal efficiency example of 85 bhp for one hour on 50 lb of 18,800 BTU per pound = 0.23; reciprocating engines are about 34 percent thermally efficient; the compression ratio raises efficiency but also the cylinder head temperature and the risk of detonation). The handbook's figure for the calculation prints 8.5 ihp where its own arithmetic uses 85. That about 34 percent (in the cylinders) less the 5 to 10 percent lost to friction leaves 25 to 30 percent is this lesson's reading, not the handbook's statement.

mediaPlan.rationale: A definition, a formula and a worked example that ties the heat balance to the horsepowers.

steps.title: Volumetric efficiency
steps.prompt: Volumetric efficiency compares the volume of charge the engine actually draws in, corrected for temperature and pressure, with the piston displacement. At standard sea-level conditions, 15 °C and 29.92 inches of mercury, a charge that exactly fills the displacement is 100 percent. A naturally aspirated engine draws in less, so its volumetric efficiency is lower. Part-throttle operation, long small-bore intake pipes and sharp bends in the induction system all reduce it. An engine with true supercharging, boosting above 30 inches, can exceed 100 percent. The course deck gives about 75 to 85 percent for a naturally aspirated engine.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 56 (volumetric efficiency as the volume of charge corrected for temperature and pressure compared with the piston displacement; standard sea level 59 °F or 15 °C, 29.92 inches of mercury; factors that reduce it; true supercharging above 30 inches may give more than 100 percent). The 75 to 85 percent typical value is from the course deck (slide 226).

mediaPlan.rationale: A definition with its standard conditions and the factors that move it.

steps.title: Propulsive and overall efficiency
steps.prompt: Propulsive efficiency is how well the engine and propeller turn brake horsepower into thrust: the thrust horsepower divided by the brake horsepower. It depends on the propeller's design, the airspeed, the altitude and the propeller speed. The overall efficiency is the combined result of them all, thermal, mechanical, volumetric and propulsive, from the fuel to the thrust. If any one is poor, say the engine breathes badly, it drags the whole chain down.
steps.note: The efficiency types follow FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 54-56 (thrust horsepower and the propeller's efficiency; thermal, mechanical and volumetric efficiency). The definitions of propulsive and overall efficiency and their key factors are from the course deck (slides 221-222 and 227-228); the handbook pages read here do not define overall efficiency.

mediaPlan.rationale: Two definitions that complete the chain of efficiencies.

steps.title: Specific fuel consumption
steps.prompt:
Specific fuel consumption says how much fuel an engine burns for each unit of power in each hour. For a piston engine it is the brake-specific fuel consumption, BSFC:

BSFC = fuel flow in lb/hr ÷ brake horsepower

An engine burning 108 lb of fuel an hour at 240 bhp has a BSFC of 108 ÷ 240 = 0.45 lb per horsepower per hour. A lower figure is better.

It is a rate for each unit of power, so engines of different sizes can be compared: the one with the lower BSFC gets more power from each pound of fuel.

If the BSFC and the power are known, the fuel flow follows: 250 bhp at 0.45 burns 250 × 0.45 = 112.5 lb of fuel every hour.

Gas turbines use thrust-specific fuel consumption, fuel flow for each pound of thrust.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 23 (the basic parameter for describing the fuel economy of aircraft engines is specific fuel consumption; for reciprocating engines it is the fuel flow in lb/hr divided by brake horsepower, called brake-specific fuel consumption; for gas turbines the fuel flow divided by thrust; comparisons can be made between various engines on a specific fuel consumption basis). The numbers (108 lb/hr, 240 bhp, 250 bhp) are invented for the example, with a BSFC of the order a piston engine has.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Fuel and efficiency calculations
steps.prompt:
Fuel flow gives endurance. An engine at 250 bhp with a BSFC of 0.45 burns 112.5 lb an hour. With 450 lb of fuel on board it runs for 450 ÷ 112.5 = 4 hours.

Efficiency is useful output divided by the energy put in. One horsepower for one hour is 1,980,000 ft-lb. A pound of fuel of 18,800 BTU gives 18,800 × 778 = 14,626,400 ft-lb of heat energy.

At a BSFC of 0.45 the engine burns 0.45 lb for each horsepower-hour:

efficiency = 1,980,000 ÷ (0.45 × 14,626,400) = 0.30, or 30 percent.

This is the brake thermal efficiency. A lower BSFC means a higher efficiency, because the same work uses less fuel.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 23 (1 hp = 33,000 ft-lb per minute = 1,980,000 ft-lb per hour), PDF p. 55 (each BTU is equivalent to 778 ft-lb; the thermal efficiency formula) and PDF p. 56 (the brake thermal efficiency example with a heat content of 18,800 BTU per pound). The BSFC route to the efficiency is the lesson's rearrangement of the handbook's formula. The numbers (250 bhp, 0.45, 450 lb) are invented for the example.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Does the answer make sense?
steps.prompt:
Before you trust a calculation, check the units and the size of the answer.

Units: write the unit beside every number and let the units cancel. Pressure in psi times area in square inches gives pounds. Times a stroke in feet gives ft-lb. Ft-lb a minute divided by 33,000 gives horsepower. If you end up with horsepower per minute, something is wrong.

Size: estimate first with rounded numbers. A 5.25 in bore is about 5, so the area is about 0.8 × 25 = 20 sq in. Times a 4 in stroke is about 80 cu in, and six cylinders about 480. The exact answer, 519.5, is close, so the sum is probably right.

Compare with what you know: 375 hp from 520 cu in is 0.72 hp per cubic inch. An answer of 3,750 or 37 hp for that engine is out by a factor of ten.
steps.note: The method of checking units and estimating the size of an answer is the lesson's own teaching. The numbers are from the GTSIO-520-H overhaul manual, PDF pp. 152 to 153 (bore 5.250 in, stroke 4.000 in, 520 cu in, 375 hp) and the PLANK units from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 51.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: What leading particulars are
steps.prompt:
An engine's leading particulars are the main facts that identify it and describe its size, its ratings and its limits. They are what you look up first on a data sheet.

They include the model designation, the arrangement of the cylinders and their number, the bore and stroke, the displacement, the compression ratio, the rated horsepower and the rated rpm, and the firing order.

There are more: the direction the propeller shaft turns, the fuel grade, the oil grade and the oil capacity, the drive ratios, the spark timing, and the temperature and pressure limits.

The legal source for an approved engine is its type certificate data sheet. The maker's manual gives the same figures for the engine in your hands.
steps.note: The term 'leading particulars' and the list are from the instructor's learning outcomes for this lesson (objectives 14 to 17) and the course deck (slide 'Engine Data Plate & Leading Particulars Interpretation', which names the type certificate data sheet as the legal specification); the handbook and manuals read here do not use the phrase. The particulars listed are those on the GTSIO-520-H detail specification pages, overhaul manual PDF pp. 152 to 153.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: The data plate and the engine's name
steps.prompt:
Every certified engine carries a permanent, fireproof data plate. It identifies the engine with at least its maker, its model and its serial number. The serial number lets you track its total time, its time since overhaul and any airworthiness directives.

The model name is a code, which lesson 5 decoded. In GTSIO-520-H the manual's general information says the engine is geared, turbocharged, fuel injected and horizontally opposed, and 520 is its displacement in cubic inches.

The H marks the variant. A limit that belongs to another variant does not apply to this one, so always check the variant before you read a figure.
steps.note: The regulatory content of the data plate (14 CFR 45.13 and EASA Part 21) and the use of the serial number are from the course deck (slide 207); the handbook pages read here do not describe the engine data plate, so the instructor should confirm the wording against the regulation. The engine's description is from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 152 (C-3-2: geared, turbocharged, six-cylinder, fuel injected, horizontally opposed, 520 cubic inches). The deck reads the letters as G for geared, TS for turbosupercharged, I for fuel injected and O for opposed.

mediaPlan.rationale: The naming rule is the content; the next steps show the real data.

steps.title: Leading particulars
steps.prompt: Here is the first page of the GTSIO-520-H's detail specifications from its overhaul manual. Find these: the power it develops and at what propeller speed; the propeller drive ratio; the bore, stroke and displacement; the compression ratio; the fuel grade; and the drive ratios of the magnetos, the tachometer and the starter. The numbers are the engine's leading particulars.

steps.title: Operating particulars
steps.prompt: The second page continues with the other drive ratios, the spark timing and plug gap, the firing order, the fuel pressures, and the limits for oil pressure, oil temperature and cylinder head temperature. It ends with the dry weight. Find the spark timing, the firing order, the maximum cylinder head temperature and the normal and maximum oil temperature.
