steps.title: Reading the numbers
steps.prompt:
The data are linked, so you can check them against each other.

The 0.667:1 propeller drive means the propeller turns at 0.667 of the crankshaft speed. At 2275 propeller rpm the crankshaft turns at 2275 ÷ 0.667 = about 3,411 rpm. The engine runs fast, and the reduction gear slows the propeller.

A six-cylinder four-stroke engine fires six times in two turns, which is once every 720° ÷ 6 = 120° of the crankshaft, in the order 1-4-5-2-3-6.

Fuel pressure is quoted at a stated manifold pressure and propeller speed, 39.5 inches of mercury and 2275 rpm. A number means something only with its conditions.
steps.note: Calculations from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 152-153 (propeller drive ratio 0.667:1; 375 horsepower at 2275 propeller rpm; firing order 1-4-5-2-3-6; maximum metered fuel pressure at 39.5 inches of mercury manifold pressure and 2275 propeller rpm) and the 720° cycle from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48. The firing order also appears in the FAA handbook as the usual six-cylinder opposed order (PDF p. 37).

mediaPlan.rationale: Worked checks that the learner can repeat on the manual page.

steps.title: Comparing two engines
steps.prompt:
Use the data to compare two engines of the same size. The GTSIO-520-H and the IO-520 both have six cylinders, a 5.25 in bore, a 4.00 in stroke and 520 cu in.

GTSIO-520-H: 375 hp at 2275 propeller rpm (about 3,411 crankshaft rpm), compression ratio 7.5:1, geared and turbocharged, 13 quart sump.

IO-520 (the -B and similar models): 285 hp at 2700 rpm, compression ratio 8.5:1, direct drive, 12 quart sump.

Power for each cubic inch: 375 ÷ 520 = 0.72 against 285 ÷ 520 = 0.55. The geared engine gets more from the same displacement, mainly by running faster and by boosting the air.

The brake mean effective pressures are close: about 168 psi and 161 psi.
steps.note: The GTSIO-520-H figures: Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 152 to 153 (375 horsepower at 2275 propeller rpm, 0.667:1, 7.5:1, 13 quarts). The IO-520 figures: IO-520 Permold Series maintenance manual, Publication M-11, PDF p. 13 (printed 1-9) for the -B, -BA, -BB, -C, -CB, -M and -MB (rated maximum continuous operation 285 brake horsepower at 2700 rpm, 8.5:1, 12 quarts, six cylinders, 5.25 in by 4.00 in, 520 cu in); the manual's design features (PDF p. 12, printed 1-8) describe a propeller flange and a wet sump and no reduction gear, and the model code has no G, so the engine is direct drive. The IO-520 is a different engine, shown for comparison only. The BMEP values are the lesson's calculation by the handbook's formula, BMEP = bhp x 33,000 / (L x A x N x K): 168 psi at 3,411 rpm and 161 psi at 2,700 rpm. The two engines also differ in firing order and spark timing (Terminologies lesson).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Calculate and explain
steps.prompt:
Take one engine, such as the GTSIO-520-H, and work out in your own words and numbers: its displacement, its compression ratio and clearance volume, its crankshaft speed at rated power, its power in kilowatts and its BMEP. Check each answer for units and size.

Then say what each kind of horsepower means, which is bigger than which, and where the rest of the fuel's energy goes. Find three leading particulars on its data sheet and the condition each is quoted for.

Then take the lesson's quiz.
steps.note: Completion step: the learner applies the formulas to the course engine (opening prompt, action, feedback, completion evidence) from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 48-56, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 152-153.

mediaPlan.rationale: The learner works the numbers for the course engine in their own words.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Power
lessons.objective: Explain why a piston engine's power changes: how altitude, temperature and humidity thin the air it breathes, and how ignition timing, spark plugs, fuel metering, induction and exhaust leaks, and low compression take power away.
lessons.purpose: Explain why actual engine output changes even when the engine itself has not fundamentally changed.
outcomes: Explain how available oxygen affects combustion and engine output.
Explain the effect of altitude on air density and naturally aspirated engine power.
Explain the effect of ambient temperature on engine performance.
Explain the effect of humidity.
Explain the concept of density altitude.
Predict the effect of a hot, high-altitude operating environment on available power.
Explain how mixture strength affects combustion and engine power.
Explain why mixture adjustment may be required as altitude changes.
Explain the influence of manifold pressure.
Explain the influence of RPM.
Explain how induction restrictions reduce power.
Explain the effect of carburettor heat on induction-air density and available power.
Explain how engine temperature and cooling condition can influence performance.
Explain how supercharging or turbocharging can compensate for altitude-related loss of induction pressure.
Predict qualitatively whether a given operating or atmospheric change will increase or reduce engine performance.
lessons.syllabusNote: The official description explicitly requires identification of factors affecting power output and performance.
lessons.completionCriteria: Sort the causes of a power loss into natural and mechanical factors; explain the effect of altitude, temperature and humidity on the oxygen each intake stroke draws in, and say what density altitude is and what a hot, high airfield does to the power; explain mixture strength and why the mixture is leaned as the aircraft climbs; explain what manifold pressure and rpm each do to the power, and how a hot or a cold engine and a boosted induction change it; and say what early or late ignition, a fouled plug, an induction or exhaust leak and a compression leak each do to the engine.

steps.title: An air breather
steps.prompt: A piston engine is an air breather. It takes in air, adds fuel, lights the charge and takes power from the expanding gas. So anything that changes the quality of the air, or the way the engine burns the charge, changes the power. Before you read on, list what you think can lower an engine's power. Then sort your list into two kinds: things nature changes, and things that can be wrong with the engine.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 37 (the typical aircraft engine is an "air breather"; anything that adversely impacts the quality of the atmosphere affects the power output; nature's variables and mechanical issues). The sort into natural and mechanical factors follows the module and the course deck (slides 229-239, 243).

mediaPlan.rationale: A prediction prompt that sets up the two groups of factors.

steps.title: Air available
steps.prompt: Change the altitude, the temperature compared with a standard day, and the humidity. Watch how much air is available to burn. Which of the three matters most? Which can you do nothing about? Then try the three example days.
steps.note: Built for this lesson from the standard atmosphere and the ideal-gas law (pressure and temperature at altitude; Charles's law as in EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 38-39; water vapour taking part of the pressure, EASA Module 16, PDF p. 39). "Air available" is the mass of dry air in the volume each intake stroke draws, as a fraction of a standard sea-level day. It is a teaching quantity, not a prediction of any engine's power.

mediaPlan.rationale: Three sliders make altitude, temperature and humidity something the learner changes and compares.

steps.title: Altitude and pressure
steps.prompt: As an aircraft climbs, the air pressure falls and the air gets thinner. It holds fewer molecules of oxygen in each unit of volume. A piston engine draws in the same volume of air on every intake stroke, whatever the altitude, so each stroke takes in less oxygen and the engine makes less power. The course rule of thumb is a loss of about 3% of the power for every 1,000 ft of climb in a naturally aspirated engine, which the interactive agrees with. A supercharged or turbocharged engine makes up the lost pressure up to its critical altitude.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 37-38 (ambient pressure falls with altitude; the air becomes rarified, with less oxygen per unit volume; each intake stroke ingests less oxygen at altitude, so the horsepower is reduced; an engine with no supercharging struggles at 15,000 ft). The 3% per 1,000 ft rule of thumb is from the course deck (slide 230) and agrees with the standard-atmosphere model used in the interactive (about 2.8% per 1,000 ft to 5,000 ft). Turbocharging is covered in Induction & Exhaust.

mediaPlan.rationale: The cause is one idea, said once, then explored in the interactive.

steps.title: Temperature
steps.prompt: Hot air is thinner than cold air. When air is heated at constant pressure its volume grows in proportion to its absolute temperature (Charles's law): 500 cu in of air at 0 °C becomes 500 × 323 ÷ 273 = 591.6 cu in at 50 °C. The engine still draws in the same volume, so the same intake stroke holds fewer oxygen molecules, and the power falls as the temperature rises. In an engine with a carburettor the mixture also becomes richer as the temperature rises, which lowers the power further.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 38-39 (Charles's law, V1 ÷ V2 = T1 ÷ T2 with the worked example of 500 cubic inches at 0 °C and 50 °C, absolute temperatures 273 and 323 K; a piston engine is a positive displacement pump, so the number of oxygen molecules entering falls as temperature rises; the mixture consumed enriches as temperature increases). Absolute temperature is the temperature in degrees Celsius plus 273.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short law with a worked number; the learner then sees it in the interactive.

steps.title: Humidity
steps.prompt: Air always carries some water vapour, and the vapour takes up room that oxygen would otherwise fill. When the humidity is high there is less oxygen per unit volume of air, so each intake stroke takes in less oxygen and the combustion of the charge is altered. The effect is small on its own: saturated air on a standard day holds about 2% less dry air. On a hot, humid day it adds to the effect of the heat, and the interactive shows a loss of about 10% at sea level.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 39 (high humidity means less oxygen per unit volume because of the space occupied by water vapour, so each intake stroke pulls in less oxygen). The figures are from the standard-atmosphere model in the interactive (Magnus formula for the vapour pressure): saturated air at 15 °C is 1.7% water vapour by pressure. The course deck (slide 233) gives a 1-3% loss.

mediaPlan.rationale: The effect and its size are stated once; the interactive shows how it combines with heat.

steps.title: Density altitude
steps.prompt:
Pressure tells you how high you are. The engine needs density, and density also depends on temperature and humidity. Density altitude combines them: it is the altitude, in a standard atmosphere, at which the air has the same density as the air you are in.

On a standard day the density altitude is the altitude itself. A hot day raises it by roughly 120 ft for each degree Celsius above standard. A humid day raises it a little more.

Take an airfield at 5,000 ft on a day 20 °C above standard. Its density altitude is about 7,300 ft. The engine breathes about 80 percent of the air of a standard sea-level day, so it loses about a fifth of its power.

That is 'hot and high': the power falls once for the height and again for the heat. The explorer now shows it.
steps.note: Density altitude: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), glossary, PDF p. 467 (the altitude in standard air at which the density is the same as that of the existing air). That a hot day raises it by roughly 120 ft per degree Celsius is a common rule of thumb; the interactive's own model (standard atmosphere and ideal-gas law) gives about 116 ft, and an airfield at 5,000 ft on a day 20 degrees above standard comes out at about 7,300 ft and 80 percent air available. The 3 percent per 1,000 ft loss is the course rule of thumb used in Altitude and pressure. The density altitude readout in the interactive was added with this lesson.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Mixture strength
steps.prompt:
The mixture ratio is the proportion of fuel to air by weight. Only about a fifth of the air is oxygen, and the fuel burns in that oxygen, so the proportion matters a great deal.

The chemically perfect mixture, with just enough air to burn all the fuel, is about 0.067 lb of fuel to 1 lb of air. It burns hottest.

Best power comes from a somewhat richer mixture, from about 0.0725 to 0.080. The extra fuel speeds the burn, adds working mass and cools the cylinder.

Best economy comes from a leaner one, about 0.060 to 0.065, which gives the power for the least fuel.

Mixtures far from these still burn, but beyond roughly 8 to 1 or 16 to 1 air to fuel the engine stops. Too lean at high power and the cylinder overheats and can backfire.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 85 to 86 (the mixture ratio is the proportion of fuel and air by weight; the stoichiometric mixture is 0.067 lb of fuel to 1 lb of air, 15:1, and produces the highest combustion temperature; from 0.0725 to 0.080 the mixtures are best power; best economy is about 0.060 to 0.065 where manual leaning is practised; mixtures as rich as 8:1 and as lean as 16:1 will burn; the engine's leanest cylinder may backfire if the mixture is too lean; cylinder-head temperature would exceed its limit and detonation would occur on a lean mixture at high power). The handbook calls the decimal the air-fuel ratio although it is pounds of fuel per pound of air; this step calls it the proportion of fuel to air.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Mixture and altitude
steps.prompt:
A carburettor meters fuel in proportion to the air flowing through it. As altitude increases the air gets thinner, and thin air flowing through the carburettor throat tends to make the mixture richer than at the ground.

So a mixture control is provided to lean the mixture and compensate for this natural enrichment. On some aircraft the pilot leans it by hand, and on others the carburettor leans the mixture automatically at altitude.

If the mixture is not leaned the engine runs richer than it needs to, which wastes fuel and, once the mixture is richer than best power, loses power. If it is leaned too far for the power in use, the cylinders run hot.

At takeoff power the mixture must be rich enough to keep the hottest cylinder cool, and it is leaned for cruise.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 84 (less air tends to make carburettors run richer at altitude than at ground level, because of the decreased density of the airflow through the carburettor throat for a given volume of air; a mixture control is provided to lean the mixture and compensate for this natural enrichment; manual and automatic systems), PDF pp. 85 to 86 (above best power the power is lost; fuel must be added in the power range to keep cylinder-head temperatures safe) and PDF p. 401 (at takeoff power the mixture must be rich enough to supply sufficient fuel to keep the hottest cylinder cool).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Manifold pressure and rpm
steps.prompt:
The cylinders and any supercharger form an air pump, and the power developed varies directly with the rate at which the engine consumes air. So manifold pressure and rpm together measure how much air the engine is using.

Manifold pressure is the average absolute pressure of the charge in the intake manifold, in inches of mercury. It depends on the throttle setting and on any supercharging. At a given rpm, a higher manifold pressure puts more air into each cylinder and gives more power.

Rpm sets how often the cylinders draw in air. At a given manifold pressure, a higher rpm means more air each minute and more power, up to the engine's limits.

A restriction in the induction, such as a clogged filter or a throttle that does not open fully, lowers the manifold pressure and so the power.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 403 (the cylinders of an engine, with any type of supercharging, form an air pump; the power developed varies directly with the rate that air can be consumed; ignoring humidity and exhaust back pressure the manifold pressure gauge and the tachometer provide a measure of engine air consumption; for a given rpm any change in power input is reflected by a corresponding change in manifold pressure) and PDF p. 50 (manifold pressure is the average absolute pressure of the charge in the intake manifold, in inches of mercury; it depends on engine speed, the throttle setting, and the degree of supercharging). That a restriction lowers the manifold pressure and so the power is the lesson's reasoning from these.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Engine temperature and cooling
steps.prompt:
An engine has a best operating temperature. Run too hot, and the charge is preheated and can burn before the planned moment, which causes detonation. Excess heat also weakens the parts and impairs lubrication, and a hot charge is thinner, so each stroke draws in less air.

Run too cold, and fuel does not evaporate and spread well and the oil does not circulate well, so the engine runs badly.

How well the engine is cooled changes its power. Baffles that leak, fins broken or clogged, and cowl flaps closed in a climb all raise the temperature. The mixture does too: lean at high power runs hot, and rich runs cool.

The cylinder head temperature gauge shows the result, so it is read as part of the power setting.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 278 (three reasons why excessive heat is undesirable: preheating of the charge and detonation, weakening of parts, impaired lubrication), PDF p. 279 (an engine can run too cold; fuel evaporation and distribution and oil circulation depend on the best operating temperature; cowl flaps) and PDF p. 283 (baffles and deflectors direct the cooling air); the cylinder-head temperature gauge and the mixture's cooling effect: PDF pp. 85, 86 and 391 to 392. That a hotter charge is thinner follows from the Temperature step of this lesson.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Spark quality and timing
steps.prompt: A spark plug needs thousands of volts to make a hot spark, and the magneto makes them itself. If the contact breaker inside the magneto is timed wrongly, the spark is weaker and the charge burns less well. Separately, the spark has to arrive at the right moment. If it is too late (retarded), the charge is still burning as the piston passes TDC, so less of the heat reaches the piston, more goes out of the exhaust, the exhaust gas temperature rises and power is lost. If it is too early (advanced), the piston absorbs more heat than intended and the charge can detonate. In an extreme case the engine can fail.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 39-40 (magneto internal timing and the e-gap; retarded timing, heat lost through the exhaust, higher exhaust gas temperature and power loss; advanced timing, detonation and, in extreme cases, engine failure), and FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48 (the ignition timing is the manufacturer's, 20° to 35° before TDC on various engines). The GTSIO-520 manual lists spark at 20° BTC for both magnetos (PDF p. 153). Timing procedures are in the manufacturer's data.

mediaPlan.rationale: Cause and effect of early and late timing read best as a short account tied to the earlier lesson.

steps.title: Spark plugs and leads
steps.prompt: The most common ignition fault is a fouled spark plug. Lead fouling is the usual kind, and it is most often found on the lower plugs: once the ceramic nose fills with lead deposit, the high voltage runs along the deposit instead of across the gap and the plug stops sparking. It shows at the pre-takeoff magneto check: the engine runs rough when the magneto that feeds the fouled plug is selected on its own. Faults on the secondary side, such as the coil, the carbon brush, the distributor rotor or the harness, make the cylinders they serve misfire and the engine run rough.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 40 (spark plug fouling, lead fouling most often on the lower plugs, found during the ignition system check before takeoff; secondary system faults cause roughness and misfiring). The magneto check is described in the accessories and maintenance lessons.

mediaPlan.rationale: A diagnostic story that connects a fault to a symptom the learner can recognise.

steps.title: Fuel metering
steps.prompt: The fuel metering system must mix fuel and air in the right proportion at the throttle setting the operator chooses, and the fuel must be broken into a fine spray so it mixes thoroughly. A wrong proportion changes the power. Typical faults: in a float carburettor, a faulty needle valve or a leaking float; in a continuous-flow fuel injection system, dirty nozzles, which cause roughness, or the wrong unmetered fuel pressure, which makes the cylinders get the wrong mixture. The GTSIO-520-H manual, for example, lists an unmetered fuel pressure of 6.0 psi at 450 propeller rpm. The adjustment has many steps and is done only from the manufacturer's data.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 40-41 (the fuel metering system must supply the right ratio and the fuel must be atomized; float carburettor defects; dirty nozzles in continuous-flow injection; incorrect unmetered fuel pressure in the Continental system) and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 153 (C-3-3: unmetered fuel pressure 6.0 psi at 450 propeller rpm). The number is given as an example of the kind of value that has to be right and is not an instruction.

mediaPlan.rationale: The faults are a list the learner connects to the mixture; the example number comes from the course engine's manual.

steps.title: Leaks, heated air and rigging
steps.prompt: The gaskets and seals in the induction system leak with time. Any induction leak changes the fuel-air mixture the engine receives and costs power, so the system is inspected for leaks. Heated air does the same: if the carburettor heat control does not reach full cold, the engine breathes warmed air, the mixture is enriched and the performance falls, which is why the rpm drops when the pilot checks the heat. Control rigging matters too. Without full throttle travel the engine cannot make full power, and a controllable-pitch propeller that cannot reach the full-rpm position will not reach takeoff rpm.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 40-41 (induction leaks alter the fuel-air mixture and reduce power; the carburettor heat control not at full cold enriches the mixture and reduces performance; lack of full throttle travel or propeller control travel). Induction troubleshooting is also in FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 133 (Figure 3-8, air leaks and restricted ducts and filters). The handbook's statements on the direction of the mixture change with carburettor heat disagree (PDF pp. 130-131), so the direction is taken here only from the EASA text.

mediaPlan.rationale: The chain from a small leak or a short control travel to a loss of power reads best as text.

steps.title: Exhaust leaks and restrictions
steps.prompt: The exhaust is the other end of the breathing path. The gaskets at the exhaust ports are prone to leaking after a time in service, and a leak disturbs the flow of the exhaust leaving the port and so the flow of air and fuel into the cylinder. A leak in the carburettor heat system makes the engine breathe exhaust fumes when the heat is applied, and the rpm drops a lot. Leaks can also let carbon monoxide into the cabin. A blocked or restricted exhaust, such as a muffler with a broken baffle, keeps burned gas in the cylinder and costs power.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 41 (exhaust port gasket leaks; a leak in the carburettor heat system causes a large rpm loss when the heat is applied; carbon monoxide in the cabin) and FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 152 (internal muffler failures restrict the flow of exhaust gases and cause partial or complete power loss). The Induction & Exhaust lesson has the system and its inspection.

mediaPlan.rationale: The exhaust faults reuse the system from the previous lesson, so a short text is enough.

steps.title: Where compression leaks
steps.prompt: At 300° both valves are closed and the piston is squeezing the charge. For the power stroke to be strong, the charge must stay in. Find the three places it can leak: past the piston rings, between the valve faces and their seats, and through the cylinder wall if it is scored. Spotlighted here are the rings, the valves and the spark plugs.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 41 (cylinder compression is needed to extract the heat energy of the charge; the piston rings and cylinder walls wear and leak; the intake and exhaust valves may become leaky). The course deck (slide 243) adds a leaky head gasket. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The compression-stroke pose with the sealing parts spotlit shows where a cylinder can lose its charge.

steps.title: Finding a compression leak
steps.prompt: A differential compression test finds the leak. Air is fed into the cylinder, and where it escapes tells you the cause: air heard coming out of the intake system is passing a leaky intake valve, air coming from the exhaust pipe is passing an exhaust valve. A borescope can then be used to look inside. Hot gas rushing through a leak burns the carbon off the valve and discolours it at that spot. A leaking hydraulic lifter can also cost power, because it cannot hold the right valve lash and so reduces how high and how long the valve opens.
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 41 (leaky valves found with the differential compression test, audible leaks from the intake system or the exhaust pipe, a borescopic inspection, discoloration of the valve at a leak; a leaky zero-lash lifter reduces the height and duration of valve opening). The test procedure and its limits are covered in the Maintenance and Servicing lesson.

mediaPlan.rationale: The diagnostic reasoning is the content; the procedure itself belongs to the maintenance lesson.

steps.title: Boost makes up for altitude
steps.prompt:
A naturally aspirated engine can only take in what the outside pressure pushes in, so its power falls as the pressure falls. A supercharger or turbocharger puts the pressure back.

A normalizing system holds the sea-level manifold pressure up to its critical altitude. Above that altitude the waste gate is fully closed and the pressure falls as it would without the turbocharger. A ground-boosted system holds more pressure than the outside air even at sea level.

For example, an engine allowed 30 inches of mercury of manifold pressure meets only about 20.6 inches outside at 10,000 ft. A turbocharger that makes up the difference holds 30 inches there, and the engine keeps its power.

Boost has a cost. Compressing air heats it, so it may need cooling, and the extra pressure raises the risk of detonation.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 131 to 135 and the Induction and Exhaust lesson (a supercharger raises the pressure of the charge; a normalizing turbocharger makes up the pressure lost with altitude up to its critical altitude; a ground-boosted system raises it above ambient; compression heats the air, and an intercooler or aftercooler takes out the heat; detonation risk, PDF p. 50). The outside pressure of 20.58 inches of mercury at 10,000 ft is the standard atmosphere (the interactive's model). The 30 inches is an example, not an engine limit.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Sort the causes
steps.prompt:
A naturally aspirated engine is delivering less power than it should. For each of these, say whether nature or the engine is the cause, what you would check first, and why, and predict whether the power goes up or down: high altitude on a hot day; a mixture that is not leaned on a climb; a low manifold pressure at the same rpm; a cylinder head that runs too hot; a rough run on one magneto at the check; a big rpm drop when the carburettor heat is applied; a cylinder with air hissing from its exhaust pipe during a compression test.

Then take the lesson's quiz.
steps.note: Completion step: the learner applies the factors to cases (opening prompt, action, feedback, completion evidence) from EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 37-41.

mediaPlan.rationale: The learner works through cases in their own words.

checks.question: Using the GTSIO-520-H manual's figure, put these parts in the order the air passes through them.
checks.hint: Start at the part that raises the pressure and end at the part nearest the cylinders.
checks.rationale: In Figure C-3-2 the turbocharger feeds the air throttle, a duct leads to the intercooler, and the intake manifold shares the cooled air between the intake tubes, one to each cylinder.

checks.question: What drives the compressor of a turbocharger?
checks.hint: Follow the energy path on the exhaust side.
answers: A turbine turned by exhaust gas
A gear train from the crankshaft
The magneto drive
checks.rationale: Exhaust gas turns the turbine, which shares a shaft with the compressor impeller. A supercharger that is driven from the crankshaft is an internally driven supercharger, not a turbocharger.

checks.question: What does a normalizing turbocharger system do?
checks.hint: Compare the pressure it holds with the pressure outside as the aircraft climbs.
answers: Makes up the pressure lost with altitude, up to its critical altitude
Raises the manifold pressure above 30 inches of mercury at sea level
Cools the cylinder heads with the exhaust gas
checks.rationale: A normalizer regains the pressure lost as the aircraft climbs, up to its critical altitude. It is not used to boost manifold pressure above 30 inches of mercury; that is a ground-boosted system.

checks.question: What is the critical altitude of a turbocharged engine?
checks.hint: It is a limit on how high the system can keep its target.
answers: The highest altitude at which it can still hold a chosen power or manifold pressure at a given speed
The altitude at which the waste gate opens fully
The altitude at which the engine must be shut down
checks.rationale: Critical altitude is the maximum altitude, in a standard atmosphere, at which a specified power or manifold pressure can still be held at a specified speed. Above it the waste gate is fully closed and the manifold pressure falls.

checks.question: Match each part of a turbocharged induction and exhaust system to its job.
checks.hint: One part acts on the exhaust side and three on the air side.

pairs.right: Decides how much exhaust gas goes through the turbine
Raises the pressure of the incoming air
Cools the compressed air before it reaches the manifold
Stops dust and other matter entering the engine

checks.rationale: The waste gate sets the turbine speed by bypassing exhaust gas, the compressor raises the air pressure, the cooler takes out the heat of compression, and the filter protects the cylinders from abrasive dust.

checks.question: Which kind of exhaust system do all turbosupercharged engines use, and why?
checks.hint: The gas must be gathered in one place.
answers: A collector system, because the exhaust must be collected to drive the turbine
A short stack system, because it gives the lowest back pressure
No exhaust system, because the turbine lets the gas out directly
checks.rationale: On a turbosupercharged engine the exhaust gas has to be collected and carried to the turbine. A collector system raises the back pressure, but the gain from turbosupercharging is greater than the loss.

checks.question: How does an exhaust leak at a clamped joint show itself?
checks.hint: Look for a mark, not for a sound.
answers: As a flat grey or sooty black streak on the pipes near the leak
As a bright blue stain on the cowling
As frost on the collector tube
checks.rationale: An exhaust leak leaves a flat grey or sooty black streak around the joint. It is usually caused by poor alignment of two mated parts, which are repositioned to make a gas-tight fit.

checks.question: Why must exhaust parts never be marked with a lead pencil or worked with galvanised tools?
checks.hint: Think about what happens to the mark when the metal gets hot.
answers: The lead or zinc is absorbed by the hot metal, softens it and causes cracks
The marks make the part heavier
The tools would rust and block the pipes
checks.rationale: When the metal is heated the lead or zinc is absorbed, changing its structure and softening it in that area, which leads to cracks and eventual failure.

checks.question: A crack opens in the heat-exchanger surface of an exhaust muff that heats the cabin. What is the main hazard?
checks.hint: Exhaust gas is poisonous.
answers: Exhaust gas, with carbon monoxide, can reach the cabin
The cabin heater will make too much heat
The exhaust will become quieter
checks.rationale: A failure of the heat-exchanger surface lets exhaust gas into the cabin heat system, a carbon monoxide hazard. The gas can also be drawn into the induction system, causing overheating and power loss.

checks.question: What can happen when baffles inside a muffler break loose?
checks.hint: Think about the gas that needs to get out.
answers: They can block the exhaust flow and cause partial or complete loss of power
They make the engine run cooler
They only make the engine quieter
checks.rationale: Pieces of internal baffling that partly or fully block the flow restrict the exhaust and can cause partial or complete engine power loss. Erosion and carbonisation under extreme heat are the usual causes.

checks.question: What is overboost?
checks.hint: It is not the same as the manifold pressure drifting up and down.
answers: Manifold pressure above the limits set for the engine, which can cause serious damage
A slow drift of manifold pressure in the controls, which does no harm to the engine
The pressure of the exhaust gas at the turbine
checks.rationale: Overboost means exceeding the manifold pressure limit for the engine. The slow drift in the controls is bootstrapping, which is not harmful to engine life.

checks.question: Why does thin air reduce the power of a naturally aspirated engine?
checks.hint: Each intake stroke draws in the same volume. Think about what that volume holds.
answers: Each intake stroke draws in the same volume, but it holds less oxygen, so less fuel can be burned
The pistons move more slowly in thin air
The spark is weaker in thin air
Thin air makes the exhaust back pressure rise
checks.rationale: The engine draws in the same volume of air on every intake stroke, but thin air holds less oxygen in that volume. The weight of the charge falls, less fuel can burn and the power falls.

checks.question: What does poor distribution of the mixture between the cylinders force the engine to do?
checks.hint: The setting must suit the leanest cylinder.
answers: Run richer overall, because the setting must be rich enough to burn in the leanest cylinder
Run leaner overall to save fuel
Run at a lower compression ratio
Run without a throttle
checks.rationale: A carburettor setting must supply a combustible mixture for the leanest cylinder. If the shares are uneven the whole engine must be set richer than it would otherwise need to be.

checks.question: What is the first duty of the exhaust system?
checks.hint: Think about what the gases are and who is near them.
answers: To protect the airframe and its occupants from the hot, noxious gases by disposing of them safely
To heat the cabin
To raise the manifold pressure
To make the engine quieter
checks.rationale: The exhaust system can do many useful things, such as driving a turbocharger or heating the cabin, but its first duty is protection against the destructive action of the exhaust gases.

checks.question: Put these parts of an opposed engine's exhaust in the order the gas passes through them.
checks.hint: Start at the cylinder and end at the firewall.
checks.rationale: The gas leaves the cylinder through its exhaust port and the down-stack, enters the collector tube on that side of the engine, and leaves through the tapered exhaust ejector at the firewall, which also draws cooling air through the engine compartment.

checks.question: What does a higher exhaust back pressure do to a naturally aspirated engine?
checks.hint: Think about the work of pushing the gas out.
answers: It makes the engine work harder to push the gas out, so it costs power
It raises the power, because the gas is held in the cylinder
It lowers the cylinder head temperature
It has no effect on a four-stroke engine
checks.rationale: The burned gas has to push against the back pressure to leave the cylinder. A higher pressure leaves more gas behind and takes more work to expel it, so power is lost. A turbocharged engine accepts a higher back pressure because the turbocharger gains more than the back pressure costs.

checks.question: During valve overlap the manifold pressure is 35 inches of mercury and the exhaust back pressure is 29 inches. What is the pressure difference, in inches of mercury?
checks.hint: Subtract the smaller pressure from the larger.
checks.rationale: 35 - 29 = 6 inches of mercury (about 3 psi), in the direction from the intake towards the exhaust. It pushes fresh charge through the cylinder and scavenges the burned gas.

checks.question: At idle the manifold pressure is 20 inches of mercury and the back pressure is 29 inches. Which way does the gas move during valve overlap on an engine with a collector exhaust?
checks.hint: The gas moves from the higher pressure to the lower.
answers: Burned gas is drawn back into the cylinder through the exhaust port
Fresh charge is blown straight out of the exhaust
Nothing moves, because both valves are open
Fresh air is drawn in through the intake pipe
checks.rationale: The manifold pressure is below the back pressure, so the pressure difference points the other way. With a collector exhaust the gas drawn back is burned gas, which contains no oxygen, so the mixture is not affected much. With an open stack it would be fresh air that leans out the mixture.

checks.question: Put the steps in the order that takes a naturally aspirated engine from a climb to a loss of power.
checks.hint: Start with the aircraft, end with the power.
items: The air pressure falls and the air gets thinner
Each intake stroke draws in fewer oxygen molecules
Less fuel can be burned and the power falls
checks.rationale: The engine draws in the same volume of air on every intake stroke, but thinner air holds fewer oxygen molecules per volume, so less fuel can be burned and the power falls.

checks.question: Match each factor to its effect on the engine.
checks.hint: Two of these come from nature and two from the engine.

pairs.right: Thinner air, so fewer oxygen molecules per intake stroke
The air expands, so each intake stroke holds less oxygen
The charge burns after TDC and more heat leaves through the exhaust
Risk of detonation and, in extreme cases, engine failure

checks.rationale: Altitude and temperature thin the air; retarded timing wastes heat through the exhaust and raises the exhaust gas temperature; advanced timing makes the piston absorb too much heat and the charge can detonate.

checks.question: 500 cubic inches of air at 0 °C is heated to 50 °C at the same pressure. What volume does it occupy?
checks.hint: Use absolute temperatures: add 273 to each Celsius temperature, then V2 = V1 × T2 ÷ T1.
checks.rationale: V2 = 500 × 323 ÷ 273 = 591.6 cu in. The engine still draws in the same volume, but this much air now holds the oxygen of the original 500 cu in, so each intake stroke takes in about 15% less.

checks.question: A naturally aspirated engine makes 200 hp at sea level. Using a loss of 3% of the sea-level power for each 1,000 ft, estimate its power at 5,000 ft.
checks.hint: Five thousand feet is five lots of 3%.
checks.rationale: Five lots of 3% is 15%, so the power is 85% of 200 hp, which is 170 hp. It is a rule of thumb for a naturally aspirated engine; real engines differ.

checks.question: Why does high humidity reduce engine power?
checks.hint: Think about what the water vapour takes the place of.
answers: Water vapour takes up space, so each intake stroke draws in less oxygen
Water makes the fuel heavier so it will not burn
Humid air is denser, which chokes the intake valve
checks.rationale: Water vapour occupies room that oxygen would otherwise fill, so there is less oxygen per unit volume and each intake stroke takes in less of it. The effect is small by itself but adds to heat.

checks.question: What happens to the exhaust gas temperature when the ignition timing is retarded?
checks.hint: Where does the heat go if the charge is still burning after TDC?
answers: It rises, because more of the heat leaves through the exhaust and less reaches the piston
It falls, because the charge burns more completely
It stays the same, because only the pressure changes
checks.rationale: With a retarded spark the charge keeps burning after the piston has passed TDC, so less heat is transferred to the piston, more is lost through the exhaust, the exhaust gas temperature rises and power is lost.

checks.question: At the pre-takeoff magneto check the engine runs rough on one magneto. What is a common cause?
checks.hint: It is the most common ignition fault, and it favours the lower plugs.
answers: Lead fouling of the spark plugs that magneto feeds
Too much fuel in the float bowl
A leaking exhaust gasket
checks.rationale: When the ceramic nose of a plug fills with lead the high voltage follows the deposit and not the gap, so the plug does not spark. Selecting the magneto that feeds it makes the engine run rough.

checks.question: The carburettor heat control does not reach full cold. What is the effect?
checks.hint: Warm air is thinner.
answers: The engine breathes warmed air, the mixture is enriched and the performance falls
The engine gets more oxygen and makes more power
The throttle travel increases
checks.rationale: Heated induction air enriches the fuel-air mixture and reduces engine performance. This is why the rpm falls when the pilot applies carburettor heat at the check.

checks.question: In a differential compression test, air is heard escaping from the exhaust pipe. Where is the leak?
checks.hint: The air goes out the way the burned gas normally leaves.
answers: Past the exhaust valve
Past the intake valve
Through the spark plug
checks.rationale: Air that escapes from the exhaust pipe is passing a leaky exhaust valve; air heard from the intake system is passing a leaky intake valve. A borescope can then be used to look at the valve.

checks.question: How can a leaking hydraulic lifter reduce engine power?
checks.hint: Think about the valve-train lesson.
answers: It cannot hold the right valve lash, which reduces the height and duration of the valve opening
It makes the camshaft turn at the wrong speed
It changes the firing order
checks.rationale: A zero-lash lifter that leaks cannot hold the correct valve lash, so the valve opens less far and for less time than the cam intends, and the engine breathes less well.

checks.question: What is density altitude?
checks.hint: It is not the height above the ground.
answers: The altitude in a standard atmosphere at which the air has the same density as the air you are in
The height of the aircraft above the ground
The altitude shown on the altimeter when it is set to 29.92
The altitude at which the air temperature is standard
checks.rationale: Density altitude combines pressure, temperature and humidity into one number: the height at which a standard atmosphere would have the same density. The engine, the propeller and the wings respond to that density.

checks.question: An airfield is 5,000 ft above sea level and the day is much hotter than standard. What does a naturally aspirated engine feel?
checks.hint: Heat raises density altitude.
answers: A density altitude well above 5,000 ft, so less power than at 5,000 ft on a standard day
A density altitude of exactly 5,000 ft
A density altitude below 5,000 ft, so more power
No change, because only pressure matters
checks.rationale: Hot air is thinner, so the density altitude is higher than the airfield's height. The engine breathes less oxygen with each stroke and makes less power: the power falls once for the height and again for the heat.

checks.question: The density altitude at an airfield is 6,000 ft. Using the course rule of thumb of 3 percent of the sea-level power lost for each 1,000 ft, what percentage of its sea-level power can a naturally aspirated engine make there?
checks.hint: Six thousand feet is six lots of 3 percent.
checks.rationale: Six lots of 3 percent is 18 percent lost, so the engine makes 82 percent of its sea-level power. It is a rule of thumb: real engines differ.

checks.question: Match each mixture to its description.
checks.hint: Think about which one burns hottest, which gives most power and which saves fuel.

pairs.right: Just enough air to burn all the fuel, about 0.067 lb of fuel to 1 lb of air; it burns hottest
A richer mixture, about 0.0725 to 0.080, giving the most power for the airflow
A leaner mixture, about 0.060 to 0.065, giving the power for the least fuel
The cylinder overheats and the engine can detonate or backfire

checks.rationale: The perfect mixture releases the most heat. A slightly richer mixture gives the most power and runs cooler; a slightly leaner one saves fuel; and a lean mixture at high power is dangerous to the engine.

checks.question: Why must the mixture be leaned as an aircraft with a carburettor climbs?
checks.hint: Think about what happens to the air flowing through the carburettor throat.
answers: Thinner air tends to make the mixture richer, so the mixture control leans it to compensate
The fuel becomes thicker at altitude
The engine needs less fuel because it is cooler
The throttle opens further at altitude
checks.rationale: Less dense air flowing through the carburettor throat makes the carburettor run richer at altitude than at ground level. The mixture control compensates for this natural enrichment.

checks.question: Ignoring humidity and exhaust back pressure, what do the manifold pressure gauge and the tachometer together measure?
checks.hint: The cylinders and supercharger form an air pump.
answers: How much air the engine is consuming, which is a measure of its power input
The temperature of the cylinders
The fuel flow to the engine
The pressure of the engine oil
checks.rationale: The power developed in the cylinders varies directly with the rate at which air can be consumed, so manifold pressure and rpm together measure the engine's air consumption and hence its power input.

checks.question: At a constant rpm, what does a higher manifold pressure do?
checks.hint: Think about how much air each cylinder takes in.
answers: More air goes into each cylinder, so the power rises
Less air goes into each cylinder, so the power falls
The cylinders fire more often
The compression ratio rises
checks.rationale: Manifold pressure is the pressure of the charge in the intake manifold. At the same rpm a higher pressure means a denser charge in each cylinder, more fuel can burn, and the power rises.

checks.question: Why does a cylinder that runs too hot risk damage and lose power?
checks.hint: Think about the charge being heated before the spark.
answers: The charge is preheated and can burn before the planned moment, causing detonation, and the hot parts and oil are harmed
The cylinder gets more oxygen when it is hot
The spark plug works better when hot
The valves open earlier
checks.rationale: Excess heat preheats the charge so that it burns prematurely (detonation), weakens the engine's parts and impairs lubrication. A hot charge is also thinner, so each stroke takes in less air.

checks.question: At 10,000 ft the outside pressure is about 20.6 inches of mercury. A turbocharger holds 30 inches of manifold pressure there. By how many inches of mercury does it raise the pressure?
checks.hint: Subtract the outside pressure from the manifold pressure.
checks.rationale: 30 - 20.6 = 9.4 inches of mercury. Without the turbocharger the engine would breathe the outside pressure; with it, the engine keeps the power it has at the higher pressure.

checks.question: A 14-cylinder engine has a bore of 5.5 in and a stroke of 5.5 in. What is its total piston displacement, to the nearest cubic inch?
checks.hint: Area = 0.7854 × bore²; one cylinder = area × stroke; then multiply by the number of cylinders.
checks.rationale: The area is 0.7854 × 30.25 = 23.76 sq in, one cylinder sweeps 23.76 × 5.5 = 130.67 cu in, and 14 cylinders sweep 130.67 × 14 = 1,829 cu in.

checks.question: Each of six cylinders has a 5.0 in bore, a 3.75 in stroke and a clearance volume of 10.5 cu in. What is the compression ratio? Give the first number of the ratio to two decimal places.
checks.hint: Swept volume = 0.7854 × bore² × stroke. Ratio = (swept + clearance) ÷ clearance.
checks.rationale: The swept volume is 0.7854 × 25 × 3.75 = 73.63 cu in. The total volume is 73.63 + 10.5 = 84.13 cu in, and 84.13 ÷ 10.5 = 8.01, so the ratio is 8.01 to 1.

checks.question: A four-cylinder, four-stroke engine runs at 2,400 rpm. Bore 5.0 in, stroke 4.5 in, indicated mean effective pressure 135 psi. What is its indicated horsepower?
checks.hint: ihp = P × L × A × N × K ÷ 33,000, with L in feet and N = rpm ÷ 2.

checks.question: A Prony brake with an arm 3.18 ft long reads 200 lb on its scale while the engine turns at 3,000 rpm. What is the brake horsepower?
checks.hint: bhp = 2π × force × arm × rpm ÷ 33,000.

checks.question: An engine has an indicated horsepower of 200 and a friction horsepower of 30. What is its brake horsepower?
checks.hint: Friction horsepower is the difference between the two.
checks.rationale: bhp = ihp - fhp = 200 - 30 = 170 hp, and the mechanical efficiency is 170 ÷ 200 = 85 percent.

checks.question: An engine develops 310 indicated horsepower but delivers only 260 brake horsepower. What is its mechanical efficiency, as a percentage to one decimal place?
checks.hint: Mechanical efficiency = bhp ÷ ihp.
checks.rationale: 260 ÷ 310 = 0.839, so the mechanical efficiency is 83.9 percent. The friction horsepower is 310 - 260 = 50 hp, lost to the friction of the moving parts, pumping and the accessories.

checks.question: The GTSIO-520-H develops 375 hp at a crankshaft speed of 3,411 rpm. Its bore is 5.25 in, its stroke 4.00 in and it has six cylinders. What is its brake mean effective pressure, to the nearest psi?
checks.hint: BMEP = bhp × 33,000 ÷ (L × A × N × K), with L in feet and N = rpm ÷ 2.

checks.question: An engine develops 1,000 brake horsepower and drives a propeller that is 85 percent efficient. What is the thrust horsepower?
checks.hint: Thrust horsepower is the brake horsepower multiplied by the propeller's efficiency.
checks.rationale: 1,000 × 0.85 = 850 thrust horsepower. It is the thrust horsepower that decides the performance of the engine and propeller together.

checks.question: Match each kind of horsepower to what it means.
checks.hint: Think about where in the engine each one is measured.

pairs.right: The power developed in the cylinders, before friction
The useful power delivered to the propeller shaft
The power used overcoming the engine's own friction
The power as thrust, after the propeller's efficiency

checks.rationale: Indicated minus friction is brake, and brake multiplied by the propeller's efficiency is thrust horsepower.

checks.question: Put these in order from the largest to the smallest for a given engine and propeller.
checks.hint: Each loses some power to the next stage.
checks.rationale: The indicated horsepower is the most, because friction is taken away to give the brake horsepower, and the propeller is less than 100 percent efficient, so the thrust horsepower is less again.

checks.question: Why is the crankshaft rpm divided by 2 when finding the number of power strokes per minute of one cylinder?
checks.hint: Think about the 720 degrees of a four-stroke cycle.
answers: A cylinder fires once in every two turns of the crankshaft
Half of the crankshaft's power is lost to friction
The camshaft turns at twice the crankshaft speed
checks.rationale: A four-stroke cycle takes two revolutions, 720 degrees, and has one power stroke, so each cylinder has one power stroke per two turns: N = rpm ÷ 2.

checks.question: In the handbook's heat distribution for a reciprocating engine, where does the largest share of the fuel's heat go?
checks.hint: Look at the largest percentage in the figure.
answers: Out with the exhaust, 40 to 45 percent
Into useful power, 25 to 30 percent
Away with the cooling fins, 15 to 20 percent
checks.rationale: About 40 to 45 percent of the heat leaves with the exhaust. Useful power is only 25 to 30 percent, the fins remove 15 to 20 percent and the oil 5 to 10 percent.

checks.question: Which engine can have a volumetric efficiency greater than 100 percent?
checks.hint: It forces more charge in than the pistons draw.
answers: One with true supercharging, which boosts the manifold pressure above 30 inches of mercury
One that runs at part throttle
A naturally aspirated engine at sea level
checks.rationale: A naturally aspirated engine draws in less than its displacement at standard conditions, so it is below 100 percent. True supercharging forces in more charge than that, so it can exceed 100 percent.

checks.question: The GTSIO-520-H develops 375 hp. What is that in kilowatts, to the nearest whole number? Use 1 hp = 0.7457 kW.
checks.hint: Multiply the horsepower by 0.7457.
checks.rationale: 375 × 0.7457 = 279.6, so 280 kW to the nearest whole number.

checks.question: The GTSIO-520-H has a displacement of 520 cu in. What is that in litres, to two decimal places? Use 1 cu in = 16.387 cm³ and 1 litre = 1,000 cm³.
checks.hint: Convert to cubic centimetres first, then to litres.
checks.rationale: 520 × 16.387 = 8,521 cm³, which is 8.52 litres.

checks.question: An engine burns 108 lb of fuel an hour while developing 240 brake horsepower. What is its brake-specific fuel consumption?
checks.hint: Fuel flow in lb/hr divided by brake horsepower.
checks.rationale: 108 ÷ 240 = 0.45 lb of fuel per brake horsepower per hour. A lower figure means better economy.

checks.question: An engine developing 200 brake horsepower has a BSFC of 0.46 lb per horsepower per hour. How much fuel does it burn in an hour?
checks.hint: Multiply the BSFC by the brake horsepower.
checks.rationale: 200 × 0.46 = 92 lb of fuel an hour.

checks.question: The engine in the last question (92 lb of fuel an hour) has 276 lb of fuel on board. How many hours can it run at that power?
checks.hint: Divide the fuel on board by the fuel flow.
checks.rationale: 276 ÷ 92 = 3 hours, ignoring any fuel that cannot be used.

checks.question: An engine has a BSFC of 0.45 lb per horsepower per hour and the fuel has a heat value of 18,800 BTU per lb (1 BTU = 778 ft-lb; 1 hp for an hour = 1,980,000 ft-lb). What is its brake thermal efficiency, as a whole percentage?
checks.hint: Efficiency is the work done in a horsepower-hour divided by the heat energy in the fuel burned in that hour.
checks.rationale: The fuel burned per horsepower-hour is 0.45 lb, which holds 0.45 × 18,800 × 778 = 6,581,880 ft-lb. The work done is 1,980,000 ft-lb, so the efficiency is 1,980,000 ÷ 6,581,880 = 0.30, or 30 percent.

checks.question: A student works out the indicated horsepower of a small four-cylinder engine as 14,460 hp. The correct answer is 144.6 hp. What is the most likely cause?
checks.hint: The answer is exactly 100 times too big.
answers: A slip with a unit or a decimal point
The engine really is that powerful
Friction was added instead of taken away
The compression ratio was too low
checks.rationale: An answer 100 times too big for a small piston engine is a warning. Check the units and the decimal places: a stroke left in inches, an unconverted pressure or a misplaced decimal point are the usual errors. Sense-checking the size catches them.

checks.question: Match each leading particular to its value for the GTSIO-520-H.
checks.hint: Look at the two specification pages in the lesson.

pairs.right: 20 degrees before top centre, on both magnetos

checks.rationale: These are leading particulars from pages C-3-2 and C-3-3 of the overhaul manual. They describe the engine's drive, its geometry, its ratings and its timing.

checks.question: The GTSIO-520-H develops its rated 375 horsepower at 2275 propeller rpm, and its propeller drive ratio is 0.667:1. At what crankshaft speed does it do so? Give the nearest whole number.
checks.hint: The propeller turns at 0.667 of the crankshaft speed.
checks.rationale: Crankshaft speed = propeller speed ÷ drive ratio = 2275 ÷ 0.667 = 3,411 rpm. The reduction gear lets the engine run fast while the propeller turns slowly enough to be efficient.

checks.question: According to the GTSIO-520-H data page, when does the spark occur?
checks.hint: Look at the second specification page.
answers: 20 degrees before top centre, on both magnetos
20 degrees after top centre, on one magneto
At top centre, on both magnetos
22 degrees before top centre, on the left magneto only
checks.rationale: Page C-3-3 lists the spark at 20° BTC on both magnetos. A general handbook gives a range of 20° to 35° across engines; the manufacturer's value is the one that applies. The IO-520 manual gives 22°, a different engine.

checks.question: The data page gives the maximum metered fuel pressure at "39.5 inches of mercury manifold pressure and 2275 propeller rpm". Why does it say that?
checks.hint: Think about what changes with power setting.
answers: A figure only means something with the conditions it is quoted for
Because the pressure never changes with power
Because the pressure is measured only in flight
Because the pressure is the same for every engine
checks.rationale: Fuel pressure depends on the power setting, so the data gives the manifold pressure and propeller speed at which the limit applies. Reading a number without its condition leads to mistakes.

checks.question: The IO-520 develops 285 hp from 520 cu in. How many horsepower is that for each cubic inch of displacement, to two decimal places?
checks.hint: Divide the power by the displacement.
checks.rationale: 285 ÷ 520 = 0.548, so 0.55 hp per cubic inch. The GTSIO-520-H gets 375 ÷ 520 = 0.72 from the same displacement.
